name: Svelte
tag: compiler-based reactive ui for fast web apps
history: 2016: Rich Harris introduced Svelte as a compiler-first UI approach. 2019: Svelte 3 made Svelte widely popular with concise component syntax. 2020: SvelteKit emerged as the official framework for routing, SSR, and full apps. 2024+: Svelte 5 shifted toward rune-based reactivity while keeping a migration path from older syntax.
why: Svelte helps teams build interactive web UIs with less boilerplate and smaller runtime overhead by moving more work to compile time. This often leads to faster apps, clearer component code, and easier onboarding for front-end developers.
challenges: Build a counter component with increment/decrement/reset buttons and a derived label ("negative", "zero", "positive"). Keep state local and reactive.
Create a signup form using two-way binding. Show inline validation messages and disable submit until all rules pass.
Fetch todos from a public API. Render loading, error, empty, and success states. Add a derived count of completed items.
Given a legacy component that uses `$:` and `export let`, migrate it to rune-based syntax while keeping behavior unchanged.
Build a small SvelteKit page with route params, data loading, and one reusable component. Include optimistic UI for one action.

name: Vue

name: Go (Golang)
tag: compiled language for concurrent networked software
history: Designed at Google by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, and Ken Thompson (work started in 2007). Publicly announced in 2009 and open-sourced soon after. Go 1.0 released in 2012 with a strong compatibility promise. Go modules became the default dependency system in Go 1.16.
why: Go helps teams ship fast, reliable backend and infrastructure software with simple syntax, built-in concurrency (goroutines/channels), strong standard tooling, and easy static-binary deployment.

Create a Go module that wraps a public REST API. Include retries with backoff, context-aware timeouts, and table-driven tests for success/error paths.
Take a CPU-heavy function, profile it with `pprof`, optimize one hotspot, then run with PGO and compare benchmark results before/after.

name: Terraform
history: Created by HashiCorp; first released in 2014. Built around declarative HCL and provider plugins. Became a default multi-cloud IaC tool through the late 2010s. From v1.5+ licensing shifted from MPL to BUSL. OpenTofu forked from pre-BUSL Terraform and continues as an open alternative.
why: Terraform lets teams define cloud and platform infrastructure as code, review changes before apply, and keep environments reproducible across dev/stage/prod.
challenges: Create one `local_file` resource. Run `init`, `plan`, `apply`, then `destroy`. Capture only the summary lines (add/change/destroy). Timebox: 15 minutes.

Use an S3 backend + DynamoDB lock table. Run `plan`, simulate a config rename, then preserve resource with a `moved` block. Explain why no recreate happened. Timebox: 35 minutes.
After apply, change one cloud setting manually in console. Run `plan`, identify drift, and restore desired state via code. Submit drift lines only. Timebox: 20 minutes.
Add a `check` block validating an output condition (for example, required tag exists). Show failing then passing plan after fix. Timebox: 20 minutes.

latestChanges: Config-driven import blocks reduce manual state-editing workflows.
Recent 1.x releases expanded native module testing via `terraform test`.
State refactoring safety improved with stronger move/import patterns.
License change (BUSL for newer releases) led to the OpenTofu community fork.

name: Nuxt (nuxt)
tag: vue framework for full-stack web apps
history: 2016: Nuxt.js started to simplify Vue server-side rendering. 2018: Nuxt 2 expanded conventions, modules, and static generation workflows. 2021: Nuxt 3 development introduced the Nitro server engine and modern architecture. 2022: Nuxt 3 became stable with Vue 3, Vite, and composable-first patterns. 2023–2024: Nuxt 3.x refined layers, rendering controls, tooling, and ecosystem modules.
why: Nuxt gives Vue teams a batteries-included way to build SEO-friendly, full-stack apps (pages, routing, data fetching, server APIs, rendering modes, and deployment) without wiring everything manually.
challenges: Create a Nuxt app with `pages/index.vue` and `pages/about.vue`. Add links between pages and verify route generation works without manual router setup.

Implement route middleware that redirects unauthenticated users from `/dashboard` to `/login`, while preserving intended destination for post-login return.

name: Vite (vite)
tag: fast frontend dev server and production bundler
history: Created by Evan You in 2020 to address slow webpack-based Vue workflows. The name "vite" comes from French, meaning "fast." It evolved from a Vue-first tool into a framework-agnostic platform via plugins. Its model: native ESM during development, Rollup-based bundling for production.
why: Vite reduces slow feedback loops in frontend projects by starting dev servers quickly, updating modules instantly with HMR, and producing optimized production bundles with minimal config. For DevOps teams, it enables faster CI builds, predictable output folders, and simpler integration with preview/deployment pipelines.
challenges: Scaffold a project with `npm create vite@latest`, run `npm run dev`, edit one component, and confirm hot updates without full reload.
Run `npm run build`, inspect the `dist` output, and identify one generated asset that appears hashed for cache busting.
Create a CI job that runs `npm ci` and `npm run build`, then stores the `dist` folder as an artifact for later deployment.
Configure Vite dev server to bind on all interfaces and test access from another device on your network.
Add one official framework plugin and explain how plugin hooks change dev/build behavior in your project.

name: Webpack
tag: a js module bundler and asset build pipeline
history: 2012: Tobias Koppers began webpack to bundle browser-focused JavaScript modules. 2017: Webpack 2 strengthened ES module workflows and tree-shaking behavior. 2018: Webpack 4 introduced mode (development/production) and more zero-config defaults. 2020: Webpack 5 added Module Federation, persistent caching, and removed automatic Node core polyfills.
why: Webpack converts many frontend files into optimized deployable bundles. It manages dependency graphs, transformations, code splitting, and cache-friendly output for reliable CI/CD releases.
